title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: You always attend your business unit's weekly leadership meeting, where you rarely speak but your absence would be noticed. Which quadrant?
options: The room — you're senior and your presence is expected
The ritual — presence is genuinely expected, but no contested judgment is being exercised
The desk — the value is in what you do with the information afterward
The queue — if you rarely speak, the meeting isn't work
questions.explanation: Presence is real; contest isn't. This is the quadrant HRBPs over-defend because it feels like relationship work, and some of it genuinely is, which is exactly why it needs the two questions rather than instinct. A makes the module's most common error: treating seniority as presence.

questions.prompt: A complex benefits cost model with one defensible answer, requiring six hours of careful work, is:
options: Contested judgment, because it's difficult and consequential
Not contested judgment — difficulty and contest are different properties, and a determinate answer isn't contested
The room, because the stakes are high
Impossible to classify without knowing who requested it
questions.explanation: Contest means reasonable people could defensibly disagree, not that the work is hard. A determinate calculation with one right answer is difficult and uncontested, which is precisely the profile where AI assistance is most valuable and least fraught.

questions.prompt: Across HR practice areas `[V]`, where has AI adoption actually concentrated?
options: Employee relations and organizational design, where the documents are richest
Evenly across practice areas, tracking overall HR headcount
Recruiting, HR technology, L&D, and employee experience — with employee relations, talent management, org design, and compliance least adopted
Compliance first, since regulatory work is most rule-based
questions.explanation: The concentration is sharp, and the least-adopted list reads like an HRBP job description. A inverts the finding. Those areas are least penetrated, partly because their data is exactly what nobody will let a vendor near.

questions.prompt: Why is "least penetrated" not the same as "protected"?
options: Because vendors will eventually build for those areas regardless of difficulty
Because your ratio moves when the work that justified the headcount compresses — the hardest work never has to be automated for the coverage math to change
Because low adoption figures are unreliable and likely undercount actual usage
It is the same — low penetration is what job security looks like in practice
questions.explanation: The module's central argument. Ratios are set by total workload, not by the hardest item in it, so "AI can't do what I do" is true and irrelevant to the budget conversation. A is plausible but is a slower and less certain mechanism than the one that's already operating.

questions.prompt: Which quadrant is most likely to be reduced by an organizational decision rather than a technical capability?
options: The queue — automation is already eating it
The room — ethical constraints could be relaxed
The desk — context handling keeps improving
The ritual — it shrinks when someone questions the calendar, which is a political event
questions.explanation: Nothing technical removes a standing meeting; a reorg does. That makes the ritual the quadrant most exposed to a decision you don't control and least exposed to a tool: the opposite of most people's intuition about it.

questions.prompt: Gartner's projection `[V]` is that the HRBP ratio could move from roughly one per 423 employees to:
options: One per 500–600 within a decade
One per 800–1,200 within one to five years
One per 2,000 within two years
No change in ratio, with the role's content shifting instead
questions.explanation: Roughly a doubling at the midpoint, on a short horizon, alongside the recommendation to replace fixed HRBP assignments with pods of strategic talent leaders. Treat the direction as real and the timing as soft, analyst projections routinely overshoot on schedule.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest counter-argument to this module's claim about compression?
options: That AI capability has plateaued and won't reach the desk quadrant
That analyst firms are financially motivated to predict disruption

That ratios are set by budget appetite and risk tolerance rather than workload — organizations have historically kept HRBP coverage above what workload math implied, because proximity to the business is itself the product
That HR headcount has never fallen in a sustained way
questions.explanation: It's the strongest because it doesn't dispute the compression. It disputes that compression determines coverage. B is worth noticing but it's an ad hominem about the source rather than an argument about the mechanism, and two independent firms agreeing weakens it.

questions.prompt: What does the module conclude is the strategic response?
options: Resist automation of HRBP work to protect headcount
Be excellent in the room quadrant and fast everywhere else — and spend recovered capacity on more room rather than more queue
Move toward recruiting or L&D, where AI adoption and investment are concentrated
Wait for the analyst timelines to clarify before changing how you work
questions.explanation: The compression is the argument *for* the rest of the track: use AI to buy back the hours that currently prevent you from being the consultative practitioner the strategic talent leader model describes. A defends the queue, which is the losing position; C abandons the quadrant where this role's actual value sits.
